title: Blueforge: MoE routing efficiency, RoPE scaling & KV batching lab
summary: Hands-on deep dive to optimize MoE routing costs and tail latency for Blueforge's Llama/Mistral/Qwen mix. Focused on RoPE scaling for mixed sequence lengths, KV prewarm and microbatching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and private/VPC deployment implications. Agreed next steps: run a 5k-prompt batch benchmark, share benchmark harness, and schedule a follow-up pilot setup call.
topics: MoE token routing cost and gating policies
RoPE frequency scaling and sequence length mismatches
Microbatching vs continuous batching for latency SLOs
8-bit/4-bit quantization implications for Qwen and Mistral
VPC/on-prem networking, KMS/HSM and audit requirements
next_steps: Michael to share benchmark harness + runbook (s3 link) by 2026-12-06
Priya to provide recommended batch/kv configs for 2k/8k seq profiles by 2026-12-08
Blueforge to send sample prompt set and traffic profile by 2026-12-04
Schedule pilot run: week of 2026-12-14 (Marcus + Redwood infra sync)
action_items: Michael Chen: upload benchmark harness and example config to s3://redwood-blueforge/benchmarks by 2026-12-06
Priya Patel: run a quick microbatch sweep (mb 1/2/4) on quantized Mistral and report p50/p95/p99 by 2026-12-08
Tom Reynolds: provide 5k anonymized prompts and target SLOs by 2026-12-04
Marcus Li: export cluster instance types and network topology for VPC testing by 2026-12-07
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Michael Chen, Priya Patel, Sofia Ruiz (Redwood) — Tom Reynolds, Anya Holt, Marcus Li, Eva Santos (Blueforge)

Summary: quick lab-style deep dive. We demo'd a microbench, discussed gating, rope scaling, and KV prewarm ideas; covered on-prem/VPC security needs.

---
[00:00] Michael Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to jump right in with the cost/latency goals you shared, Tom — can you recap target SLOs?
[00:22] Tom Reynolds: yeah sure, target is 95% under 200ms for user-facing completions, mixed payloads, around 1M tokens/day, and we'd like cost per 1k tokens to be under our current baseline by ~30% if possible.
[00:38] Michael Chen: got it. Priya and I prepared a short lab to show routing behaviors — especially for your MoE workloads where token routing is the main cost driver.
[01:05] Priya Patel: quick note — our gating defaults send roughly 1.4 experts per token for your moefied Llama variant, so routing overhead is non-trivial. If we tune the gate threshold you can trade off a small quality drop for a big cost saving.
[01:28] Anya Holt: by "experts per token" do you mean average dispatched experts across the batch? we've seen variance in tails where some requests go to 3 or 4 experts spiking costs.
[01:45] Priya Patel: exactly. average vs tail — the cost model should account for p99 routing. you can use token affinity to pin hot tokens to a smaller expert subset which reduces variance.
[02:13] Marcus Li: how intrusive is token affinity to model outputs? customers worry about hallucination shifts when you pin routing.
[02:29] Priya Patel: good question — in our tests for Qwen we saw measurable but small shifts with aggressive affinity; the safety net is A/B evals and an automatic rollback policy in the runtime. we'll attach eval prompts.
[02:52] Sofia Ruiz: also note that affinity often pairs well with prefix KV caching — if the same prefix hits the same expert set, the KV cache warms and you avoid recompute.
[03:18] Tom Reynolds: let's talk about RoPE — our product mixes short chat (64-256) and long doc (4k-8k). we saw quality cliffs when we move to longer seqs, and latency blows up.
[03:40] Priya Patel: yeah, the classic RoPE frequency mismatch. if you train at N=2048 and serve at 8k, the positional angles wrap and you get weird decays. we recommend linear RoPE scaling or using decay-aware interpolation.
[04:05] Anya Holt: can you explain "linear RoPE scaling" quickly? I thought RoPE is fixed per embedding dim.
[04:18] Priya Patel: sure — simplest approach is to scale the position indices by factor alpha when computing cos/sin so the frequencies match target sequence length distribution. it's an approximation but often reduces the cliff. downside: might slightly change local attention patterns.
[04:41] Michael Chen: to add, we also use adaptive RoPE schedules in the runtime — on request we rescale depending on predicted sequence horizon; it's a knob we can expose.
[05:01] Marcus Li: any measurable hit to latency when doing rescale at inference?
[05:09] Priya Patel: negligible — it's just a precompute factor; the heavy work is still attention. the main latency is from KV cache misses and MoE routing spikes.
[05:28] Tom Reynolds: about KV prewarm — our users often do multi-turn dialogs with soft prefixes. When the model hits a rare long context, startup p99 is awful.
[05:43] Priya Patel: exact scenario we prepared for. two levers: prefix-splitting and KV prewarm. prefix-splitting breaks the context into chunks and preloads KV for the chunk most likely to be reused; prewarm proactively fills KV for predicted next tokens for known flows.
[06:10] Anya Holt: can you share the microbench numbers you mentioned?
[06:16] Priya Patel: yes — we ran a 1k prompt synthetic set: baseline (no affinity, no prewarm) on Mistral-xx: p50=90ms, p95=240ms, p99=420ms. with token affinity + KV prewarm: p50=82ms, p95=140ms, p99=160ms. cost per 1k tokens dropped ~25%.
[06:49] Eva Santos: those p99 improvements are big — what's the tradeoff in quality?
[06:55] Priya Patel: small BLEU-style drop (we used our internal eval suite), 0.6-1.2% depending on prompt; for many UX flows it's acceptable but recommend eval on your real prompt set.
[07:15] Michael Chen: next, quantization — Blueforge asked about 8-bit vs 4-bit for Qwen and Llama.
[07:27] Priya Patel: for Qwen-style weight layouts, 8-bit dynamic quant gives near-native perplexity for most tasks. 4-bit (and advanced FP4 schemes) can reduce memory/cost further but require per-layer calibration and sometimes per-head matmuls patching. We saw Mistral degrade more on naive 4-bit.
[07:53] Anya Holt: does Redwood runtime support mixed quant per-layer? like 8-bit for attention, 4-bit for FFN?
[08:01] Priya Patel: yes — we have per-layer quant profiles, and the optimizer can compile a hybrid kernel set. it's slightly more complex to manage but often the best balance for cost/quality.
[08:18] Marcus Li: any known perf cliffs with Qwen memory layout when using 8-bit kernels?
[08:25] Priya Patel: Qwen's block layout is friendly to 8-bit kernels, but if you force 4-bit without kernel fusion you can lose throughput due to extra dequant op overhead. our compiler picks kernels to minimize dequant cost.
[08:46] Tom Reynolds: thanks. now networking/VPC/on-prem: our security team (Eva) needs KMS integration and audit logs, plus a plan for HSM down the line.
[08:59] Eva Santos: exact. we also need retention control and SOC 2 artifacts.
[09:08] Michael Chen: we can run Redwood Private in your VPC — the control plane still may be hosted if you prefer, or fully air-gapped on prem. KMS/HSM integrations supported: we have an HSM plugin and can rotate keys. audit logs are exportable to your SIEM. we'll attach the compliance pack.
[09:36] Eva Santos: are there network-level latency tradeoffs if we keep everything in our VPC?
[09:42] Priya Patel: your network egress is basically the only added hop — with colocated GPU nodes inside the VPC it's minimal. the bigger issue is disk I/O for model weights if you use a slow NFS; we recommend NVMe local for model shards.
[09:59] Marcus Li: noted. what's the recommended instance profile for MoE + KV heavy workloads?
[10:07] Priya Patel: for MoE with 4–8 experts active typical, we recommend A100/RTX9000 class or equivalent with 80GB; multi-GPU sharded with NVLink helps. for cost-sensitive, smaller instances with more aggressive affinity + quant can work.
[10:30] Michael Chen: ok let's walk through the bench we ran just now — I have a short demo of the harness with a small Qwen mix.
[10:45] [screen share noise, faint typing]
[11:10] Priya Patel: here is the harness: it simulates your traffic mix (60% short chat, 30% doc summarization, 10% retrieval-augmented). config has gating threshold, affinity profile, kv prewarm flags, and quant profile.
[11:38] Tom Reynolds: can the harness also export per-route cost breakdown? we need token-level attribution.
[11:44] Michael Chen: yes, by default it outputs per-token cost, per-expert dispatch rate, and per-request p50/p95/p99 latency. we can map that to your billing units.
[12:03] Anya Holt: I saw in your earlier notes "rope-adaptation"—did you implement an adaptive RoPE mode in the runtime?
[12:12] Priya Patel: yes, it's experimental but in our internal builds. it selects a scale factor based on the incoming sequence length histogram and either rescales positions or switches to an alternative relative position embedding for very long contexts. we toggled it in the bench for the long-doc flow.
[12:37] Marcus Li: curious, did you test this against ALiBi?
[12:43] Priya Patel: we compared — ALiBi avoids positional wrap and is stable for long seqs but tends to change generation characteristics. For minimal changes we prefer RoPE rescale; for pure long-form stability some teams move to ALiBi-like schemes and retrain.
[13:03] Tom Reynolds: what's the recommended rollout path? enable rescale in canary, run evals, then wide?
[13:10] Michael Chen: yep — canary + A/B with automatic fallback is standard. Redwood Console can automate canary windows and quantitatively flag regressions in the eval suite.
[13:29] Eva Santos: for compliance, can the canary run be isolated to a VPC with no egress to host?
[13:35] Sofia Ruiz: yes — you can pin canary to private nodes only; the control plane telemetry can be forwarded to your SIEM without payload egress.
[13:51] Anya Holt: back to batching — you mentioned microbatching vs continuous batching. what are tradeoffs for interactive flows?
[13:59] Priya Patel: microbatching (small, user-level batches) reduces latency for single-shot chat but lowers GPU utilization. Continuous batching is throughput-optimal for high-throughput backends but increases tail latency. The sweet spot is adaptive batching: start with microbatches for low load, then expand batch window slightly when latency budgets allow. We can tune the max batch latency per route.
[14:32] Michael Chen: Priya, can you run through the config we recommend for Blueforge short vs long routes?
[14:38] Priya Patel: short routes: max_batch_latency=20ms, microbatch_size=1–4, affinity=medium, kv_prewarm=false (unless repeating prefixes). long routes: max_batch_latency=80ms, microbatch_size=8–16, affinity=low (to avoid over-constraining), kv_prewarm=true for known prefixes. quant_profile: 8-bit baseline, per-layer hybrid for FFN if memory issues.
[15:08] Tom Reynolds: good, what about MoE gating thresholds? numbers please.
[15:13] Priya Patel: start gating threshold at 0.7 for your Llama-MoE blend; that usually yields ~1.6 experts/token. Increase to 0.85 to hit ~1.2 experts/token but validate quality. For production we'd run a sweep.
[15:32] Anya Holt: can Redwood auto-sweep gating in production? like a safe optimizer?
[15:39] Michael Chen: yes — we have Optimize module which can run controlled sweeps and rollback on metric regressions. we'll include suggested sweep ranges in the harness.
[15:52] Marcus Li: about quantized kernels — what happens to memory footprint when using KV caches in 4-bit setups?
[15:59] Priya Patel: KV cache memory is mostly FP16/FP32 depending on the caching mode — quantizing weights doesn't necessarily change KV size. we have a sparse-KV compaction option which compresses KV to lower precision when possible, but it can increase decode overhead.
[16:20] Eva Santos: so KV is still the big memory consumer. if we want more KV we need larger GPUs or sharded KV?
[16:27] Priya Patel: exactly — sharded KV across GPUs helps, and we can do KV eviction policies based on frequency. we recommend hot-tiering with local NVMe for very large caches.
[16:45] Tom Reynolds: ok let's open the lab results we ran earlier — the harness output shows routing histograms.
[16:52] [typing, brief pause]
[17:10] Priya Patel: here's a routing heatmap — you can see most tokens hit 1–2 experts, but tails at 3–4 show spikes correlated with long prompt prefixes. affinity reduces that tail by ~40%.
[17:32] Anya Holt: can you export that heatmap as csv? we'll ingest into our cost model.
[17:37] Michael Chen: yes we'll push CSV and a small dashboard json to the s3 bucket.
[17:49] Marcus Li: one more infra question — for private deployment, does Redwood require any custom kernel modules or special OS images?
[17:57] Sofia Ruiz: no special kernel modules; we ship a validated image for on-prem with tuned drivers, and for VPC there's a lightweight agent. If you want air-gapped installs we provide an installer bundle.
[18:14] Eva Santos: what's the timeline for SOC 2 docs?
[18:19] Michael Chen: we'll attach SOC 2 summary and SOC2 audit vendor report to the compliance pack by next business day.
[18:28] Tom Reynolds: cool. any gotchas with multi-region routing if we activate fallback to another region for capacity?
[18:35] Priya Patel: main gotcha is KV locality — if you route to another region you lose local KV and have cold starts. our smart routing prefers region-local model variants; fallback used for burst but with best-effort caching. you can also replicate hot KV sets across regions at cost.
[18:57] Anya Holt: replication cost would blow our budget though.
[19:01] Priya Patel: understood — that's why affinity + local caching tends to be more cost-effective for steady-state.
[19:12] Michael Chen: we've been talking a lot — I want to flag recommended artifacts we'll share: bench harness, config templates, gating sweep plan, compliance pack, and a per-route cheat sheet.
[19:28] Tom Reynolds: perfect. question from Eva: HSM integration steps?
[19:33] Michael Chen: steps: 1) exchange HSM certs/ACLs, 2) Redwood deploys HSM plugin in control plane (or in your VPC), 3) key rotation policy setup. we'll attach a one-pager.
[19:53] Eva Santos: good. I'm also concerned about logging — can syslogs be forwarded encrypted to our SIEM without storing in Redwood long-term?
[19:59] Sofia Ruiz: yes, you can configure short retention and immediate forwarding; payload-level logging can be disabled.
[20:12] Anya Holt: for follow-up can we run the 5k prompt benchmark on our infra snapshot? we'll provide instance specs.
[20:22] Priya Patel: yes, we'll mirror your instance types in our bench and run both hosted and private configs. Michael will share the harness.
[20:33] [longer pause, miscellaneous questions about eval shards]
[21:05] Tom Reynolds: small nit — in your earlier bench the p95 moved a lot when we enabled affinity; can you show the exact config?
[21:13] Priya Patel: sure — affinity: mode=token_affinity, bucket_size=128, affinity_strength=0.8, gating_threshold=0.75, kv_prewarm=true, prewarm_window=16 tokens. we'll include exact YAML.
[21:36] Marcus Li: will affinity help retrieval-augmented cases where the prefix is dynamic?
[21:43] Priya Patel: for dynamic prefixes, affinity is less effective but still helps if you use hashing on retrieval keys rather than raw token strings. we recommend hybrid: affinity for stable prefixes, recency-based KV for dynamic retrieval flows.
[22:02] Anya Holt: good call.
[22:07] Michael Chen: okay let's capture quick runbook steps for pilot: 1) Blueforge provides prompt set and infra snapshot, 2) Redwood uploads harness and suggested configs, 3) Redwood runs bench in-canary with metric collection, 4) joint review and gating sweep, 5) pilot rollout.
[22:35] Tom Reynolds: timeline looks fine.
[22:40] Eva Santos: any blockers from Redwood side for the on-prem install?
[22:45] Michael Chen: no blockers; we just need your network ACLs and disk perf numbers. Marcus will share those.
[22:55] [some chatter about calendar invites]
[23:12] Anya Holt: quick question — do you support runtime policy that automatically reduces experts per token when cost > threshold?
[23:20] Priya Patel: yes, dynamic cost-based routing is something we've prototyped as a policy: it shifts gating threshold up during cost spikes for a given route, while flagging quality regressions. We can enable as an experimental policy.
[23:40] Marcus Li: that might be useful for holiday traffic spikes.
[23:46] Michael Chen: we'll add it to the Optimize playbook for your account.
[24:00] [brief pause]
[24:12] Tom Reynolds: any final security question — can we run canary inside our DMZ?
[24:18] Sofia Ruiz: yes, canaries can be pinned to any network boundary you choose.
[24:25] Eva Santos: ok good.
[24:32] Michael Chen: wrapping up — we will: send harness, send compliance pack, prepare gating sweep ranges, and schedule pilot week. Priya will run microbatch sweep and attach results.
[24:48] Tom Reynolds: thanks, this was helpful. appreciate the concrete numbers.
[24:54] Anya Holt: thanks everyone.
[25:00] Michael Chen: thanks all — we'll follow up with artifacts.

(Transcript continues with Q&A, short interruptions and side-chat; trimmed for brevity)

References and attachments mentioned: s3://redwood-blueforge/benchmarks (will be populated), https://docs.redwood.ai/private-deploy-checklist.pdf (compliance pack), example YAML: redwood://configs/blueforge-gating-sweep.yml

End of transcript.
